operationalization: Compare physiological thermal limits and transplant performance beyond range edges against realized geographic range boundaries, or compare transplant survival with and without competitors excluded at range margins; the claim is supported if most species survive climatic conditions beyond their natural boundaries when competitors are absent.

candidate_datasets.name: GlobTherm
candidate_datasets.role: Global database of species thermal tolerance limits to compare physiological climatic limits with realized geographic boundaries

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF (Global Biodiversity Information Facility)
candidate_datasets.role: Species occurrence records to determine realized geographic and climatic range edges

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: Gridded climate variables at range margins to match with physiological thermal tolerances

obstacles: Realized vs fundamental niche comparisons using physiological lab measurements may not capture extreme episodic weather events in the wild.
Direct experimental competitor-removal studies across range edges are compiled for only a subset of terrestrial and marine taxa.
rationale: Comparing physiological thermal limits (e.g. GlobTherm) with realized climatic limits (GBIF + WorldClim) and published transplant meta-analyses directly tests whether climate alone sets range boundaries. However, lab thermal tolerances are imperfect proxies for lifetime survival under field weather extremes, and multi-factor transplant datasets cover only a modest sample of species.

operationalization: Measure phenotypic selection gradients (regressions of relative survival and reproductive success on heritable trait values) across wild populations; non-zero directional and stabilizing selection gradients confirm that advantageous variations are preserved and injurious ones eliminated.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository (Kingsolver et al. phenotypic selection datasets)
candidate_datasets.role: Compiled datasets of standardized linear and quadratic selection gradients across hundreds of wild plant and animal populations

candidate_datasets.name: SPI-Birds Network and Database
candidate_datasets.role: Individual-level longitudinal life-history, morphological, and reproductive success records in wild bird populations

obstacles: Part of the statement defines the term 'Natural Selection', while the empirical component requires separating genetic covariance from environmental covariance between traits and fitness.
Available selection gradient compilations are biased toward short-term studies of terrestrial vertebrates, insects, and annual plants.
rationale: While naming the process 'Natural Selection' is definitional, the underlying claim that heritable trait variation systematically covaries with differential survival and reproduction in nature has been extensively quantified via Lande-Arnold selection gradients. Large open compilations of selection gradients exist, though coverage is taxonomically uneven and environmental confounds can bias unmanipulated observational estimates.

operationalization: Test whether conspicuous intraspecific polymorphisms in wild populations exhibit selection gradients indistinguishable from zero and allele/morph frequency trajectories consistent with neutral genetic drift, as opposed to balancing or frequency-dependent selection.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Selection gradient compilations and time-series morph frequency datasets for polymorphic species

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA)
candidate_datasets.role: Population genomic polymorphism data comparing synonymous (nearly neutral) versus nonsynonymous site diversity

obstacles: Statistical failure to reject a zero selection gradient in finite samples cannot easily distinguish strict neutrality from weak or fluctuating selection.
Many classical visible polymorphisms that Darwin referred to are actually maintained by balancing selection rather than neutrality, whereas molecular neutrality requires modern reinterpretation.
rationale: At the molecular level, neutral variation remaining polymorphic is readily tested with population genomic data, but that requires reinterpreting Darwin's visible morphological characters. For visible morphological polymorphisms, time-series and fitness datasets exist, though distinguishing strict neutrality from fluctuating or frequency-dependent selection has moderate discriminating power.

operationalization: Query global alien species inventories across all countries and biogeographic regions to test whether every region has established, self-sustaining populations of non-native species that successfully compete with or displace native biota.

candidate_datasets.name: GRIIS (Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species)
candidate_datasets.role: Country-by-country checklists of introduced and naturalized species across the globe

candidate_datasets.name: GloNAF (Global Naturalized Alien Flora)
candidate_datasets.role: Global database of naturalized alien vascular plant occurrences across over 1,000 regions

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF (Global Biodiversity Information Facility)
candidate_datasets.role: Global occurrence records documenting establishment and spread of naturalized species

obstacles: Establishment of introduced species is often facilitated by anthropogenic habitat disturbance or enemy release (absence of coevolved parasites) rather than superior intrinsic adaptation to the undisturbed native environment.
rationale: Darwin explicitly operationalizes his claim through the universal establishment of naturalized foreign species across countries. Comprehensive global datasets (GRIIS, GloNAF) directly cover practically all countries and confirm widespread naturalization. The main limitation in discriminating power is that invasion success can reflect enemy release or human disturbance rather than superior adaptation per se.

operationalization: Compare predation rates by visual predators on prey individuals or models that match versus mismatch their natural background substrate across field studies and meta-analytic compilations; lower attack or mortality rates on background-matching phenotypes confirm the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Published field experiment and meta-analysis datasets on camouflage, background matching, and avian predation rates on insects and birds

candidate_datasets.name: Zenodo
candidate_datasets.role: Archived multispectral image analysis and survival datasets testing crypsis in ground-nesting birds and folivorous insects

obstacles: Human visual assessment of colour matching differs from UV-sensitive avian predator vision, requiring calibrated multispectral or predator-vision-modelled datasets.
Field predation experiments using artificial prey models may not capture behavioural posture and microhabitat choice of live prey.
rationale: The protective value of background-matching coloration against visual predators is straightforward to operationalize via differential predation rates on matching versus non-matching prey. Numerous experimental datasets and meta-analytic compilations in public repositories (Dryad, Zenodo) directly measure survival and attack rates across insects and birds with strong discriminating power.

operationalization: Estimate additive genetic variances and cross-age genetic correlations for traits expressed at distinct ontogenetic stages (e.g. larval vs adult traits), and compare rates of adaptive divergence across life stages in clades with complex life cycles; high stage-specific heritability with low cross-stage genetic correlation and independent evolutionary divergence confirm the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Quantitative genetic datasets of ontogenetic genetic covariance matrices (G-matrices) and comparative datasets of larval versus adult morphological evolution

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: Stage-specific gene expression and phenotypic data across larval, pupal, and adult stages in Drosophila

obstacles: Pleiotropy and genetic correlations across life stages can constrain completely independent adaptation even when stage-specific variation exists.
Quantitative genetic pedigree datasets measuring traits across multiple life stages in the wild are available for a limited set of model and well-studied taxa.
rationale: Darwin's claim combines two testable propositions: age-specific inheritance (positive genetic variance within stages and imperfect genetic correlation across stages) and independent adaptive evolution of larval and adult forms. Both quantitative genetic G-matrix datasets and comparative phylogenetic datasets for holometabolous insects and amphibians exist on Dryad, though taxonomic breadth for wild quantitative genetics is moderate.

operationalization: Perform phylogenetic comparative analyses across animal clades (e.g. mammals, birds, beetles) testing whether polygynous mating systems significantly predict the presence and relative size of male weaponry (antlers, horns, spurs, enlarged mandibles) and intensity of male-male combat.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Comprehensive morphological dataset across all bird species to pair with mating system and spur/weapon data

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: Species-level life-history, mating system, and dimorphism data for mammals

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative datasets on mammalian horn/antler weapons, mating systems (e.g. Lukas & Clutton-Brock), and male combat intensity

obstacles: Categorical classifications of social mating systems (monogamous vs polygamous) can mask genetic extra-pair paternity and continuous variation in the opportunity for sexual selection.
Some weapons also function in anti-predator defence, requiring control for female weapon presence and predation regime.
rationale: This comparative prediction maps cleanly onto cross-species datasets of mating systems and male weaponry. Large open datasets for mammals and birds allow phylogenetic generalized least squares or logistic regressions within days, and confounding functions like anti-predator defence can be controlled by comparing male-specific presence against female traits.

operationalization: Combine estimates of directional female mate-choice selection gradients on male song and plumage with additive genetic variance estimates in wild birds, and test phylogenetically whether clades with strong female choice exhibit elevated evolutionary rates of plumage and acoustic divergence.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Global avian trait database for comparative analyses alongside plumage dichromatism datasets

candidate_datasets.name: xeno-canto
candidate_datasets.role: Global repository of bird sound recordings used to quantify acoustic complexity and divergence across species

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Published datasets of avian plumage colouration (e.g. Dale et al.), mate-choice selection gradients, and phylogenetic trees

obstacles: Directly observing thousands of generations of wild bird evolution is impossible, requiring macroevolutionary comparative inference combined with microevolutionary selection gradients.
Plumage and song divergence are also shaped by species recognition, sensory drive from habitat acoustics/lighting, and predation risk.
rationale: While 'thousands of generations' cannot be observed directly in real-time longitudinal bird datasets, the mechanism can be tested by combining microevolutionary data (female preference gradients and heritability of ornaments) with macroevolutionary rate analyses across avian phylogenies using global plumage and song repositories (xeno-canto, Dryad). Sensory drive and natural selection on signalling create partial confounds.

operationalization: Across animal species where males and females occupy the same foraging niche and habitat, test whether indices of sexual dimorphism in size, structure, and colour are strongly predicted by mating system and operational sex ratio rather than minor residual ecological differences.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological and ecological foraging niche data across birds

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits
candidate_datasets.role: Foraging strata and diet attributes for world birds and mammals to identify species with shared general habits

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative datasets of avian and mammalian sexual size and colour dimorphism paired with mating system data

obstacles: Fecundity selection on females (e.g. larger body size for clutch/litter production) and sex-specific parental care roles can drive sexual dimorphism even when foraging habits are identical.
Existing global trait databases rarely record sex-specific diet or microhabitat partitioning at fine resolution.
rationale: Comparative datasets allow testing how much variance in sexual dimorphism among ecologically similar sexes is explained by sexual selection proxies (mating system, extra-pair paternity). However, fecundity selection on females and subtle ecological niche divergence between sexes are difficult to fully disentangle using coarse species-level trait databases.

operationalization: Test for reciprocal phenotypic selection gradients and correlated geographic/phylogenetic trait matching between floral tube/spur dimensions and insect pollinator proboscis lengths across populations and sister taxa.

candidate_datasets.name: Web of Life Ecological Networks Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global plant-pollinator interaction networks

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Floral morphology traits across plant species

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Population-level datasets of floral tube length, pollinator proboscis length, and reciprocal selection gradients

obstacles: Comparative trait matching alone cannot easily distinguish simultaneous reciprocal coevolution from sequential unilateral tracking ('one after the other') where one partner adapts to a pre-existing trait of the other.
Reciprocal fitness measurements on both the plant and the insect partner in the same populations are available for only a handful of model systems.
rationale: Darwin explicitly allows that mutual adaptation may occur 'either simultaneously or one after the other'. Trait-matching datasets across populations and phylogenies, along with phenotypic selection studies on floral traits, are publicly available on Dryad, though datasets measuring fitness consequences on the insect side are much scarcer.

operationalization: Examine the distribution of phenotypic effect sizes of adaptive Quantitative Trait Loci (QTLs), beneficial mutations, and chromosomal/structural variants (including polyploidy and major-effect loci) underlying adaptive divergence; the strict claim that selection acts *only* on infinitesimally small modifications is refuted if large-effect mutations or saltational changes (e.g. whole-genome duplications, major-effect loci) regularly contribute to adaptation.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Compiled QTL effect-size distributions and adaptive mutation datasets across wild plants, animals, and experimental evolution studies

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI BioProject / GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Genomic datasets documenting adaptive major-effect loci (e.g. Eda in sticklebacks, wing-pattern supergenes in Heliconius) and polyploid speciation in plants

obstacles: The Beavis effect (upward bias in estimated QTL effect sizes in small mapping populations) can inflate apparent effect sizes of detected loci.
What counts as 'infinitesimally small' versus 'large sudden change' lies along a continuum, though extreme cases (whole-genome duplication, major homeotic/supergene shifts) are clear.
rationale: Remembering that resolvability scores testability rather than truth, Darwin's strict universal claim ('only by... infinitesimally small inherited modifications') makes a strong empirical prediction about the effect-size distribution of adaptive variants. Existing QTL compilations, experimental evolution datasets, and genomic studies of major-effect adaptive mutations and polyploid speciation directly test (and largely refute the strict 'only' form of) this claim.

operationalization: Compare survival, growth rate, and fecundity (fitness components) between inbred/selfed progeny and outcrossed progeny (across strains or varieties) across plant and animal species; significantly higher fitness in outcrossed progeny (heterosis) and lower fitness in inbred progeny (inbreeding depression) confirm the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Large meta-analytic datasets of inbreeding depression and heterosis across hundreds of wild and domestic plant and animal species

candidate_datasets.name: MaizeGDB (Maize Genetics and Genomics Database)
candidate_datasets.role: Extensive phenotypic records comparing inbred lines and hybrid crosses for vigour and yield

obstacles: Crosses between very distantly related varieties or incipient species can occasionally exhibit outbreeding depression due to Dobzhansky-Muller incompatibilities or disruption of local adaptation.
rationale: Inbreeding depression and hybrid vigour (heterosis) are among the most directly measurable and thoroughly documented phenomena in quantitative genetics and evolutionary biology. Massive open datasets from agricultural breeding trials, wild pedigree studies, and cross-species meta-analyses allow an immediate, high-power test.

operationalization: Use population genomic linkage disequilibrium, heterozygosity, and coalescent analyses across obligately selfing hermaphrodites and asexual lineages to test whether any lineages persist over geological timescales ('an eternity of generations') without any outcrossing or genetic exchange, and compare extinction rates of strict selfers against outcrossers.

candidate_datasets.name: Tree of Sex Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global database of reproductive systems, selfing rates, and sexual systems across plants and animals

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA)
candidate_datasets.role: Population genomic data for selfing hermaphrodites (e.g. Caenorhabditis elegans, Arabidopsis thaliana) and ancient asexual candidates (e.g. bdelloid rotifers, oribatid mites)

obstacles: Darwin's phrase 'for an eternity of generations; perhaps at very long intervals' makes the timescale open-ended, requiring phylogenetic age estimation and genomic detection of rare historical recombination.
Distinguishing rare outcrossing from gene conversion or horizontal gene transfer in genomic data requires careful bioinformatic filtering.
rationale: Modern population genomics and phylogenetic comparative datasets (such as the Tree of Sex database and genomic studies of selfing plants, nematodes, and putative ancient asexuals) directly test whether strictly self-fertilizing lineages ever persist long-term without occasional outcrossing. Indeed, genomic evidence consistently reveals rare outcrossing in selfing hermaphrodites and high macroevolutionary turnover of strict selfers.

operationalization: Cross-tabulate plant growth form (tree vs shrub/herb) against sexual system (dioecious/monoecious vs hermaphroditic flowers) across global and regional angiosperm floras, controlling for phylogenetic non-independence across orders; a significantly higher proportion of dioecy/dicliny in trees confirms the pattern.

candidate_datasets.name: Tree of Sex Database
candidate_datasets.role: Species-level sexual system classifications across thousands of angiosperm species

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Plant growth form (woodiness, tree habit) and floral sexual system traits

candidate_datasets.name: GIFT (Global Inventory of Floras and Traits)
candidate_datasets.role: Regional floras and functional traits including growth form and reproductive traits across global regions including Britain and Australia

obstacles: While the correlation between tree habit and separate sexes is directly testable, verifying whether wind/insect pollen movement between trees vs within large crowns is the primary causal driver requires ecological pollination models.
rationale: The empirical generalization that trees have separate sexes (dioecy/dicliny) more frequently than herbaceous plants is one of the best-known macroecological correlations in plant reproductive biology. Global trait databases (Tree of Sex, TRY, GIFT) cover tens of thousands of plant species across all orders and regions, enabling an immediate and definitive statistical test.

operationalization: Test across experimental evolution populations of varying census sizes and wild species with varying effective population sizes ($N_e$) whether larger populations exhibit faster rates of fitness increase and higher rates of adaptive substitution ($\alpha$ or $\omega_a$) due to increased supply of beneficial mutations.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA)
candidate_datasets.role: Polymorphism and divergence genomic datasets across species with varying effective population sizes to estimate adaptive substitution rates

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Experimental evolution datasets manipulating population size and mutation rate, and comparative McDonald-Kreitman datasets across animals and plants

obstacles: In comparative genomic datasets, effective population size ($N_e$) affects both the supply of new beneficial mutations and the efficacy of selection against slightly deleterious mutations, which must be separated via DFE-alpha methods.
In very large populations, clonal interference among competing beneficial mutations can decelerate the rate of adaptation in asexual microbes.
rationale: Darwin's statement directly anticipates mutation-limited adaptation where the rate of beneficial mutation appearance scales with population size ($N \mu$). Both laboratory experimental evolution datasets (directly varying $N$ and $\mu$) and comparative population genomic datasets (testing the correlation between $N_e$ and adaptive substitution rates $\omega_a$) are publicly available and directly test this mechanism.

operationalization: Compare lineage diversification rates, phenotypic evolution rates, directionality of colonization (continent-to-island vs island-to-continent), and global invasion success between species originating in large continental regions versus small isolated regions or islands.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF (Global Biodiversity Information Facility)
candidate_datasets.role: Global geographic range sizes and native/introduced distributions of terrestrial species

candidate_datasets.name: GloNAF (Global Naturalized Alien Flora)
candidate_datasets.role: Naturalization success and geographic spread of continental versus island plant species

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife
candidate_datasets.role: Time-calibrated phylogenies of terrestrial vertebrates to compare diversification rates and biogeographic dispersal directionality

obstacles: The claim bundles three predictions (faster modification on large areas, wider spread of large-area forms, and producing the most new species), which do not always covary—island radiations often show rapid per-lineage morphological modification despite continental species dominating global spread.
Area correlates with habitat heterogeneity and climate stability, confounding pure competitive-superiority explanations.
rationale: The sub-claims about geographic spread (continental species invading and spreading more widely than island species) and total species production are readily testable with global biogeographic, phylogenetic, and invasion databases (VertLife, GloNAF, GBIF). However, because island lineages often exhibit faster short-term phenotypic evolution rates while continental clades dominate broad-scale spread and total richness, the composite claim is partially resolvable with nuanced components.

operationalization: Compare speciation rates, extinction rates, mean lineage age, and morphological evolutionary rates among freshwater, marine, and terrestrial clades using time-calibrated molecular phylogenies and the fossil record.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database (PBDB)
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrences coded by environment (freshwater, marine, terrestrial) to estimate origination and extinction rates

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Habitat classification (freshwater vs marine) and species richness for all ray-finned and cartilaginous fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Time-calibrated phylogenies of fishes and invertebrates comparing diversification and phenotypic rates between marine and freshwater realms

obstacles: Freshwater habitats are highly fragmented into isolated river basins and lakes rather than acting as a single small basin, which actually drives rapid allopatric speciation in many teleost groups (e.g. cichlids, ostariophysans) contrary to Darwin's premise.
Taphonomic preservation rates in freshwater sediments differ substantially from marine shelf environments.
rationale: Macroevolutionary rates (speciation, extinction, lineage age) across freshwater, marine, and terrestrial realms can be directly compared using large phylogenetic datasets (e.g. Rabosky et al. fish trees on Dryad, FishBase) and the Paleobiology Database. While freshwater habitats do harbour ancient relict lineages (lungfishes, gars), modern comparative data also allow testing whether overall freshwater diversification is actually slower or faster than marine diversification.

operationalization: Fit evolutionary mode models (stasis, random walk, punctuated shifts, directional trend) to co-occurring fossil lineage time series within regional stratigraphic sections to test whether morphological change is slow, episodic, and asynchronous across species in the same region.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database (PBDB)
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence data for co-occurring fossil lineages

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Compiled paleontological morphological time-series datasets (e.g. Hunt et al.) testing stasis, random walks, and directional evolution

obstacles: 'Very slowly' is scale-dependent: contemporary selection studies show rapid generation-to-generation evolution, whereas paleontological time series show long periods of stasis punctuated by episodic change.
High-resolution stratigraphic sections tracking multiple co-occurring lineages simultaneously with morphometric data are restricted to select marine microfossil and lacustrine deposits.
rationale: Paleontological morphometric time series (compiled by Hunt and colleagues on Dryad) allow quantitative model selection among stasis, intermittent shifts, and continuous directional change, while contemporary selection studies test short-term rates. However, ambiguity in what constitutes 'very slowly' across ecological versus geological timescales and limited multi-species co-occurring morphometric series make it only partially resolvable.

operationalization: Test in paleontological time series whether geographic occupancy and site abundance systematically decline in the time bins preceding a taxon's last appearance, and in contemporary ecological time series whether population declines and range contractions precede local extinction as competing taxa increase.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database (PBDB)
candidate_datasets.role: Taxon occurrence counts and geographic occupancy per geological time bin prior to extinction

candidate_datasets.name: BioTIME
candidate_datasets.role: Global database of biodiversity time series tracking species abundance trajectories and local extirpations in ecological communities

candidate_datasets.name: Living Planet Database
candidate_datasets.role: Vertebrate population abundance time series documenting declines toward rarity and extirpation

obstacles: In the fossil record, sampling and preservation biases (the Signor-Lipps effect) can create an artificial pattern of apparent decline before extinction if not corrected with occupancy/sampling standardization.
Declines to rarity can be driven by abiotic environmental change rather than competitive displacement by favoured forms alone.
rationale: The proposition that rarity precedes extinction and that increasing abundance of favoured competitors coincides with declines of less favoured ones can be tested directly in both fossil occurrence databases (PBDB, using sampling-standardized occupancy trajectories) and modern community time series (BioTIME). Standard paleobiological and ecological methods handle sampling biases, though disentangling competitive displacement from abiotic drivers limits discriminating power slightly.

operationalization: Test whether competition coefficients in experimental communities and extinction probabilities during biological invasions or clade replacements are negatively correlated with phylogenetic distance (i.e. congeneric or closely related species suffer stronger competitive suppression or higher local extirpation).

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database (PBDB)
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil taxon co-occurrence and extinction records to test whether origination of new congeneric species elevates extinction rates of close relatives

candidate_datasets.name: BioTIME
candidate_datasets.role: Long-term ecological community time series to test whether increases in newly arriving or expanding species disproportionately depress congeneric abundances

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Meta-analytic datasets testing the phylogenetic limiting similarity hypothesis (competition strength vs phylogenetic distance)

obstacles: Close relatives share similar environmental tolerances (habitat filtering), which creates positive co-occurrence patterns in observational data that can mask competitive exclusion.
Tracking competitive extermination specifically 'during the progress of formation' of an incipient variety in the wild is rarely captured in standard datasets.
rationale: Darwin's phylogenetic limiting similarity and competitive exclusion hypothesis has been tested in experimental competition meta-analyses, invasion datasets, and paleontological clade-replacement studies available on Dryad and PBDB. However, shared habitat requirements among close relatives confound observational co-occurrence patterns, and observing suppression specifically during incipient speciation is difficult.

operationalization: Regress total community biomass, productivity, or total individual abundance ('amount of life') on functional trait diversity and phylogenetic diversity across experimental biodiversity manipulations and natural community plots; a positive effect of functional/structural diversity on total biomass confirms the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Cedar Creek Ecosystem Science Reserve LTER
candidate_datasets.role: Long-term grassland biodiversity experiments directly measuring plot biomass across gradients of species and functional group diversity

candidate_datasets.name: ENA / Jena Experiment datasets (via PANGAEA)
candidate_datasets.role: Experimental grassland plots manipulating plant species richness and functional trait diversity to measure community biomass

candidate_datasets.name: sPlotOpen
candidate_datasets.role: Global open-access vegetation plot database paired with TRY functional traits to relate structural diversity to vegetation cover/biomass

obstacles: Most direct experimental manipulations of structural diversity focus on terrestrial herbaceous plants, whereas trophic and animal community biomass datasets are mostly observational.
rationale: This is the foundational 'biodiversity-ecosystem functioning' (BEF) hypothesis, which Darwin himself linked to experimental turf plots. Decades of large-scale experimental datasets (Cedar Creek LTER, Jena Experiment on PANGAEA) and global observational plot databases (sPlotOpen) directly measure community biomass as a function of functional and phylogenetic diversification.

operationalization: Calculate species-to-genus ratios (S/G) and standardized effect sizes of Mean Nearest Taxon Distance (MNTD) or Mean Pairwise Distance (MPD) in small-scale co-occurring quadrat plots compared against regional species pool null models; taxonomic/phylogenetic overdispersion at fine spatial scales confirms the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: sPlotOpen
candidate_datasets.role: Over 95,000 georeferenced vegetation plots globally to test taxonomic and phylogenetic dispersion at fine plot scales

candidate_datasets.name: ForestGEO
candidate_datasets.role: Stem-mapped forest census plots allowing spatial point-pattern analysis of whether immediate nearest-neighbour trees belong to different genera and orders

candidate_datasets.name: GrassPlot
candidate_datasets.role: Fine-grain Palearctic grassland plot records across spatial scales from square centimetres to square metres

obstacles: Environmental filtering at intermediate scales often causes closely related species to co-occur (phylogenetic clustering), opposing the competitive overdispersion predicted at the finest neighbourhood scales.
Taxonomic ranks (genus, order) are somewhat arbitrary across clades, though continuous phylogenetic distance provides an objective modern equivalent.
rationale: Darwin's claim is the direct precursor to community phylogenetics and species-to-genus ratio tests on small plots. Massive fine-grain vegetation plot databases (sPlotOpen, GrassPlot) and stem-mapped forest plots (ForestGEO) allow testing whether immediate physical neighbours belong to different genera/orders or show phylogenetic overdispersion relative to null expectations.

operationalization: For regional floras worldwide, compare the observed ratio of newly added alien genera to newly added alien species against null models that randomly draw the same number of species from the global flora; also test whether alien species without native congeners naturalize at higher rates (Darwin's naturalization hypothesis).

candidate_datasets.name: GloNAF (Global Naturalized Alien Flora)
candidate_datasets.role: Regional lists of naturalized alien vascular plant species and genera across >1,000 regions globally

candidate_datasets.name: GIFT (Global Inventory of Floras and Traits)
candidate_datasets.role: Native regional floras (species and genera counts) to pair with alien floras for proportional comparison

candidate_datasets.name: World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP)
candidate_datasets.role: Standardized global plant taxonomy and native/introduced status by botanical country

obstacles: A mathematical sampling artefact exists: adding a small sample of species from a larger global pool to a regional flora naturally yields a higher genus-to-species ratio than the larger native flora unless evaluated against an explicit random-draw null model.
Human introduction bias (horticultural preference for novel exotic genera) influences which alien species are introduced prior to naturalization.
rationale: Known in ecology as 'Darwin's Naturalization Hypothesis', this claim has been extensively tested. Global databases of native and naturalized floras (GloNAF, GIFT, WCVP) contain the exact variables needed across hundreds of regions, allowing both a literal replication of Darwin's proportional calculation and rigorous null-model phylogenetic tests within days.

operationalization: Using high-resolution fossil clades with species-level phylogenies and stratigraphic ranges, test whether ancestral morphospecies and intermediate phenotypes persist alongside their derived daughter species (budding speciation with long ancestral persistence) or go extinct shortly after daughter lineages originate and expand.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database (PBDB)
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic first and last appearance data for ancestor-descendant candidate pairs and sister species in the fossil record

candidate_datasets.name: Triton (Planktonic Foraminifera Database)
candidate_datasets.role: High-resolution global Cenozoic planktonic foraminiferal occurrences with well-resolved ancestor-descendant lineages

obstacles: Taxonomic pseudoextinction (anagenetic renaming of an evolving lineage) can be confused with true competitive extinction of a persisting parent species after cladogenesis.
Only groups with exceptionally dense fossil records (e.g. planktonic foraminifera, marine molluscs, mammals) allow reliable identification of ancestor-descendant persistence.
rationale: In paleobiology, ancestor-descendant persistence during budding cladogenesis versus competitive replacement can be tested in densely sampled fossil clades (such as Cenozoic planktonic foraminifera in Triton and well-sampled invertebrates/mammals in PBDB). However, separating true competitive extinction from taxonomic pseudoextinction and abiotic turnover limits discriminating power.

operationalization: In discrete morphological character matrices containing both fossil (stem-group) and extant (crown-group) taxa, ordinate taxa in multivariate morphospace and measure whether older extinct taxa occupy regions intermediate between extant orders/families and decrease morphological gap sizes between living clades.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Public repository of hundreds of morphological character matrices combining fossil and extant taxa across vertebrates, invertebrates, and plants

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database (PBDB)
candidate_datasets.role: Geological age and taxonomic assignments for extinct taxa included in morphospace analyses

obstacles: Fossil preservation leaves missing entries for soft-tissue characters in morphological matrices, which can pull incomplete fossils toward the origin of ordination spaces if not handled with distance metrics robust to missing data.
Circularity must be avoided by measuring raw character-state intermediacy in morphospace rather than relying solely on a tree topology built under cladistic assumptions.
rationale: Morphospace occupation analyses using discrete and continuous character matrices archived on MorphoBank directly test whether extinct taxa fall between extant groups in character space (without needing to assume a tree topology). Hundreds of published cladistic matrices spanning tetrapod, arthropod, echinoderm, and plant evolution are openly downloadable for immediate morphospace ordination.

operationalization: Test whether morphological and genetic distances scale continuously with divergence time across intraspecific populations/subspecies, congeneric species, and distinct genera, and whether the major axes of intraspecific phenotypic covariance ($\mathbf{P}$ or $\mathbf{G}$) align with the directions of interspecific and intergeneric divergence.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Individual-level and species-level morphological measurements across bird subspecies, species, and genera

candidate_datasets.name: BOLD (Barcode of Life Data System)
candidate_datasets.role: Intraspecific, congeneric, and intergeneric genetic distance distributions across hundreds of thousands of animal and plant species

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative morphometric datasets testing alignment between intraspecific variance-covariance matrices and macroevolutionary divergence

Taxonomic rank definitions (variety, species, genus) vary somewhat across taxonomic traditions.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database (PBDB)
candidate_datasets.role: Global stratigraphic first and last appearances of fossil orders, families, genera, and species across the Phanerozoic

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA)

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Meta-analytic datasets of reciprocal transplant, common garden, and reaction norm studies in plants and animals

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database

operationalization: Test across oceanic island bird lineages whether pectoral muscle and wing reduction evolve via neutral mutation accumulation under relaxed selection ('disuse' in a modern genetic sense) versus directional positive selection ($dN/dS$, selection scans, metabolic energy savings) correlated with absence of mammalian predators and resource limitation.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF (Global Biodiversity Information Facility)

obstacles: A fossil gap remains between non-volant insectivorous laurasiatherian ancestors and the earliest known Eocene bats (*Onychonycteris*), which already possessed powered flapping flight alongside primitive climbing/gliding limb proportions.
Soft-tissue wing membranes (patagia) are preserved only in exceptional Lagerstatten.
rationale: Morphometric, phylogenetic, and aerodynamic datasets for early Eocene fossil bats (*Onychonycteris*, *Icaronycteris*) and extant bats/gliding mammals are available in MorphoBank, MorphoSource, and Dryad. These datasets allow rigorous testing of whether the uropatagium is ancestral in Chiroptera and whether stem-bat limb proportions fall along a gliding-to-flapping biomechanical trajectory, though the pre-*Onychonycteris* fossil gap limits complete resolution.

operationalization: Map ecological/behavioural traits (e.g. terrestrial vs aquatic foraging stratum, ground vs arboreal habits) and corresponding anatomical structures (e.g. foot webbing, zygodactyl toe morphology, beak shape) onto time-calibrated phylogenies to identify lineages where behavioural niche transitions precede anatomical loss or modification (behavioural drive / phylogenetic lag).

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Global morphological dataset paired with trophic and foraging lifestyle classifications across all birds

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits
candidate_datasets.role: Foraging stratum (water, ground, bark, canopy) and diet data for all extant bird and mammal species

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife
candidate_datasets.role: Time-calibrated phylogenies of all birds and mammals to reconstruct the relative timing of behavioural versus morphological transitions

obstacles: Continuous partial modifications of bone proportions (e.g. longer tarsi in ground-foraging woodpeckers or reduced webbing in Hawaiian geese) often accompany behavioural shifts, even while major qualitative characters (webbed feet, picid skull/zygodactyly) are retained.
rationale: Combining global ecological/foraging databases (EltonTraits, AVONET) with morphological measurements and time-calibrated phylogenies (VertLife) allows immediate identification and phylogenetic reconstruction of mismatches between ancestral morphology and derived habits (including Darwin's exact examples of terrestrial Anatidae and ground-foraging Picidae like *Colaptes*).
